title: The AI-Enhanced Deliverable
text:
The exercise asks for AI-driven enhancements to the one-page slide from Part 1, in a format that can be embedded in a website. The enhancement is the interactive map — live at https://www.kaseyzapatka.com/cascadia/reports/map.html — the slide’s static hero map, rebuilt with AI as an explorable Leaflet map — hover any hex for its plan-enabled units, toggle the 3,419 underlying opportunity parcels, turn the Mountain Line routes on and off, click any parcel for its details. It is a single self-contained HTML file, so it embeds in any web page — including a client-facing one — with one line of code.
AI was also used to build the delivery vehicle: this Quarto website, which packages the enhanced map together with the Part 1 slide (download), the full data story, and the methods audit trail — so the deliverable arrives polished and is easy to transmit to clients for review. The site renders from a public repository, republishes automatically on every push, and every number regenerates from one command (Rscript code/run_all.R).

title: The AI-Enhanced Deliverable
text:
How AI was used
The exercise asks for AI-driven enhancements to the Part 1 deliverable, and that is where I used it. I designed and built the analysis — the capacity framework, the opportunity screen and its exclusion rules, the hot-spot methodology, and the pipeline behind them. Claude (Anthropic) was then used to enhance and harden the deliverable:

Enhancing the slide’s hero map into the interactive map — the Leaflet build, the hover and toggle behavior, and the self-contained packaging that makes it embeddable.
Building this website in Quarto — the pages, navigation, theme, and publishing workflow that package all three parts into a polished deliverable a client can review from a single link.
Auditing the code — reviewing the pipeline for correctness and reproducibility, and checking the cartography programmatically, including colorblind-safety validation (deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia) of the palette before it touched a map.

What stayed human: the choice of story (plan-enabled capacity, not another choropleth), the framing against the Growth Policy rather than zoning, the analysis and its assumptions, the exclusion rules and their ethics, the recommendations, and the final read on every number before it shipped.

title: The AI-Enhanced Deliverable
text:
Why this transparency matters
A firm that publishes AI-polished work owes its clients clarity about where the analysis ends and the polish begins. Everything quantitative on this site traces to the reproducible pipeline in the repository; the AI acceleration is documented here; and the assumptions that drive the headline numbers are inspectable in one file (code/00_setup.R). That is the standard I would bring to client work.

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Plan-enabled capacity
For each parcel whose Growth Policy designation calls for housing:

capacity = developable acres × assumed du/ac − existing units, floored at zero

where developable acres = acres × (1 − max(flood share, slope share)). Taking the max of the two constraint shares is conservative without double-counting (their overlap is unknown).
Allowable densities come from the adopted Our Missoula 2035 Growth Policy designation ranges, as those ranges are applied in the City’s own annexation and rezoning staff reports (e.g., “Residential Medium Density (3 to 11 dwelling units per acre)… Residential High Density (24 to 43 dwelling units per acre) (Our Missoula 2035)”). Capacity uses the midpoint of each range — a deliberately conservative “expected” density rather than the plan’s ceiling:

Urban Center has no du/ac in the Policy; it is pinned at 43 — the highest density the Policy quotes anywhere — which is conservative for the downtown designation. Values are centralized in code/00_setup.R. All other designations (including the Sxwtpqyen Area’s own designation, industrial, parks, open/resource) contribute zero capacity — a conservative choice that likely understates the total.

title: Methods & Sources
Methods & Sources
text:
Plan vintage
The taxlot layer carries the future land-use designations of the 2035 Growth Policy. In December 2024 the City adopted the successor Our Missoula 2045 Land Use Plan (need identified: ~22,000–27,500 new homes by 2045). Capacity here is therefore measured against the 2035-vintage map and read as a feasibility check on the 2045 target — designation-level densities are broadly continuous between the two plans, but a designation-by- designation re-run on the 2045 map is the natural refresh once its GIS layer is in hand.

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH)
NOAH = parcels with at least one dwelling unit whose total assessed value per unit falls in the bottom quartile of the city’s housing stock — everything under ~$240,300 per unit (6,691 parcels, ~23,800 units). Assessed value proxies price level, not rent, and lags the market; the flag marks relative affordability, not income-qualified affordability. Exposure is measured on the hex grid: a hex’s NOAH units count as exposed when the hex is, or touches, a 95%+ capacity cluster (~2,600 units).

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Transit accessibility
Stops and route shapes come from Mountain Line’s published GTFS feed (July 2026; data/external/). A parcel counts as transit-accessible when it intersects a quarter-mile (1,320 ft) Euclidean buffer around any stop — the standard walkshed shorthand, which slightly overstates true network walking distance. 58% of plan-enabled units on opportunity parcels fall inside the walkshed.

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Hot-spot analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*)
Plan-enabled units on opportunity parcels are summed to a 1,000-ft hexagonal grid (~20-acre cells; 1,188 hexes contain at least one housing-eligible parcel). Gi* runs on the hex values with queen contiguity, self-inclusive weights; classes are reported at 90/95/99% confidence.
Significance and multiple testing. With 1,188 hexes, fixed z-score thresholds involve many simultaneous tests: at the 95% level, ~30 hexes would clear the bar by chance alone, against 40 observed — so the 95% tier is treated as an outer envelope, not headline evidence. The finding rests on the 99% tier: 29 hexes observed against ~6 expected by chance (~11,400 units). Under a one-sided false-discovery-rate correction (q < 0.05), 25 hexes (~10,800 units) remain significant — the concentration conclusion is unchanged. Gi* here uses the analytic normal approximation (no permutations), read as descriptive spatial inference rather than formal hypothesis testing.
Why hexes rather than parcels? Parcel-level unit gap is extremely right-skewed (median 1, maximum ~3,200), and parcels vary enormously in size, so a parcel-level statistic mostly re-identifies individual mega-parcels and their immediate neighbors. Aggregating first asks the policy-relevant question — which places, at the scale of a block cluster, concentrate capacity — and yields legible corridors instead of scattered outliers. A uniform grid also equalizes the spatial support underlying each observation (parcels differ in area by four orders of magnitude), which contiguity-based weights otherwise distort.
Why Gi* rather than a LISA map? The question this analysis asks is specific: where do high-capacity places sit next to other high-capacity places — LISA’s high-high quadrant. A Gi* hot spot is precisely that: because the statistic sums each hex together with its neighbors, a significant positive z-score can only occur where high values cluster against other high values. So Gi* delivers the high-high answer directly, with a single confidence-graded class that maps cleanly.
LISA (local Moran’s I) reports the same high-high clusters but adds three more classes — low-low, and the high-low / low-high spatial outliers. Those are valuable diagnostics (an isolated mega-parcel in a low-capacity neighborhood is a high-low outlier), but for a policy audience they quadruple the legend to answer a question nobody asked here. The one thing LISA would add — cold spots (low-low) — turns out empty: no low-capacity cluster reaches significance in this data, which is why the map legend shows only capacity clusters. Running LISA as a robustness check on the hex grid is a natural QC step for the regional expansion.

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Cluster naming
The three labeled clusters on the maps are contiguity components of the 95%+ hexes; their names were verified by reverse-geocoding each component’s centroid (North Reserve corridor; Halle Drive area = Linda Vista / Miller Creek; Hillview Way / Moose Can Gully = South Hills).

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Reproducibility
Rscript code/run_all.R   # raw .gdb -> derived data -> figures -> map
Numbered scripts with all assumptions centralized in code/00_setup.R; the exact package environment is recorded in output/session_info.txt. The website is rendered with Quarto from the committed figure and map outputs, so rendering never re-runs the analysis.

title: Methods & Sources
text:
Limitations

Plan-implied, not predicted. Capacity measures what the adopted future land-use map makes room for — not ownership, feasibility, or infrastructure timing.
Densities are range midpoints, not the plan’s ceiling — using the top of each designation range would roughly double the headline capacity. Urban Center’s value is an assumption (the Policy states no du/ac for it).
Assessed values proxy economic softness; they lag the market and compress at the top.
The Sxwtpqyen Area (766 parcels) is conservatively excluded from capacity; the Mullan-area master plan is largely residential, so totals are understated.
Zoning is not analyzed here — the story is deliberately framed against the Growth Policy. A zoning-vs-plan entitlement-gap analysis is the natural next phase.
ACS estimates (tenure, rent burden) carry margins of error; figures cited are point estimates for Missoula city.
The walkshed is Euclidean, not network-routed, and GTFS reflects current service.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
text:
NoteExecutive Summary



Missoula is considering policy changes to advance housing affordability and smart growth as it rewrites its development code under the 2023 Montana Land Use Planning Act. The adopted Our Missoula 2045 Land Use Plan sets the target: roughly 22,000–27,500 new homes by 2045.
The finding: The City does not need to find new land or amend its plan to hit that target — it can add roughly 43,000 homes by removing the conversion friction between what the adopted plan already allows and what gets built. Vacant and economically underbuilt parcels provide ground for ~43,000 homes at conservative midpoint densities — the 2045 target, 1.6 to 2 times over — netting out floodway and steep-slope acres. Half of that capacity is small-scale infill on parcels of five acres or less; the strongest clusters (99% confidence) hold a quarter of it on ~2% of the urban fabric; 58% of it is within a quarter-mile of a bus stop. The binding constraint is not land; it is conversion friction: zoning that has not caught up with the plan, review process, and infrastructure timing.
The recommendation: Align zoned entitlements with the Growth Policy where the capacity clusters — the North Reserve corridor, Linda Vista/Miller Creek, and the South Hills — make small infill by-right, and pair that upzoning with preservation for the ~2,600 lowest-cost homes that sit in the same growth path.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
text:
Approach
We work from the City of Missoula taxlot layer — 32,974 parcels with existing use, dwelling units, assessed values, current zoning, Growth Policy future land use, and floodplain/steep-slope shares1. For every parcel whose future land-use designation calls for housing, we compute plan-enabled capacity: the parcel’s developable acres (net of floodway and steep slope) times an assumed allowable density for its designation, minus the dwelling units already standing2.
We then keep only parcels where that capacity is realistically addressable: vacant, or economically soft (assessed improvements worth less than the land under them), excluding public and institutional land, parks and open space, master condo records — and mobile-home parks, which score as “soft” but are naturally occurring affordable housing (they get their own finding below, as a risk rather than an opportunity). Finally, a Getis-Ord Gi* analysis on a 1,000-ft hex grid finds where that capacity clusters. Full detail: Methods & Sources.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
section: Finding 1 — The capacity concentrates in a few corridors
text:
Finding 1 — The capacity concentrates in a few corridors






Figure 1: Green hexes hold significantly more plan-enabled capacity — counting each hex together with its neighbors — than a random arrangement of the same parcels would produce (Getis-Ord Gi*); darker green means stronger statistical evidence, not more capacity. The three biggest clusters — labeled and verified by reverse-geocoding — are the North Reserve corridor, the Linda Vista/Miller Creek area, and the South Hills. The 29 hexes at 99% confidence alone hold ~11,400 units — a quarter of the citywide total on ~2% of the urban fabric.



Untapped capacity is not evenly distributed across the city. Aggregated to a 1,000-ft hex grid and tested for spatial clustering, 29 of 1,188 hexes (~2.4%) are capacity clusters at 99% confidence — five times as many as chance would produce — and they hold ~11,400 of the ~43,000 plan-enabled units. Widening to the 95%+ envelope adds 11 hexes for ~14,600 units; the concentration finding is robust to a false-discovery-rate correction (see Methods). These are the places where code reform, infrastructure investment, and permitting capacity would do the most work per acre: the North Reserve corridor, the Linda Vista/Miller Creek area, and the South Hills, with smaller significant clusters through midtown. The capacity is also transit-aligned in a measurable sense: 58% of all plan-enabled units sit within a quarter-mile walk of one of Mountain Line’s 334 bus stops (agency GTFS) — growth where zero-fare transit already runs.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
section: Finding 2 — The plan already makes room for ~43,000 homes
text:
Finding 2 — The plan already makes room for ~43,000 homes






Figure 2: Dwelling units by Growth Policy future land-use designation: homes on the ground today (blue) versus today plus plan-enabled capacity on vacant and underbuilt parcels (green). Community Mixed Use and the medium/high residential designations carry most of the headroom.



Summing across designations, 3,419 opportunity parcels (~4,200 acres) carry ~43,000 plan-enabled units — nearly a one-for-one doubling of the existing ~44,300-unit stock3. Roughly half of that capacity sits on vacant land and half on economically underbuilt parcels whose improvements are worth less than the land beneath them. This is not a rezoning wish list: every unit is consistent with the future land-use map the City has already adopted, on acreage that nets out floodway and steep-slope land.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
section: Finding 3 — Half the opportunity is small-scale infill
text:
Finding 3 — Half the opportunity is small-scale infill






Figure 3: Plan-enabled units by parcel size and current condition. Small parcels (≤ 5 acres) — the scale of an individual owner, a small builder, a neighborhood lot — carry half the citywide total.



Large vacant tracts draw most of the attention, but the volume sits elsewhere: parcels of five acres or less carry ~23,100 units — 54% of the total, most of it on underbuilt rather than vacant land. The distinction matters for policy design: large-site capacity is unlocked by master planning and infrastructure; small-site capacity is unlocked by by-right approvals, missing-middle allowances, and simpler review — exactly the levers a development-code rewrite controls.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
section: The affordability lens — ~2,600 of the city’s lowest-cost homes sit in the growth path
text:
The affordability lens — ~2,600 of the city’s lowest-cost homes sit in the growth path
Missoula is a majority-renter city: 52% of households rent, and half of those renters (49.9%) are cost-burdened, paying more than 30% of income for housing (ACS 2019–2023). More housing where demand already is would ease that pressure for a large share of the city.
The risk is that new development displaces the cheap housing that already exists. We flag the city’s lowest-cost stock — the bottom quartile by assessed value per unit, under roughly $240,000 (~23,800 units) — as naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) and map it against the capacity clusters: ~2,600 of those units sit inside or beside the growth path.






Figure 4: Blue hexes shade where the low-cost stock concentrates; dark-green outlines are the 95%+ capacity clusters from the hero map. The overlap is where displacement pressure would concentrate: ~2,600 low-cost units sit inside or directly adjacent to a capacity cluster.



The most exposed class is mobile homes — 530 parcels (~2,850 units) on land the Growth Policy designates for higher density, which is why they are excluded from the opportunity count entirely. The implication is sequencing: pair upzoning from the start with preservation tools — resident-ownership conversions, NOAH acquisition funds, zoning overlays — in exactly the hexes where the two maps overlap.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
section: What this means for the code reform
text:
What this means for the code reform

Align zoning with the plan where capacity clusters. The North Reserve, Linda Vista/Miller Creek, and South Hills clusters are where the gap between the future land-use map and current entitlements costs the most homes. Start the rewrite there.
Make small infill easy. Half the capacity is on small parcels; by-right missing-middle allowances and streamlined review are the levers that convert it into permitted homes.
Protect the residents already providing affordability. Preservation for the 530 mobile-home parcels before — not after — the surrounding land appreciates.

title: Missoula’s Housing Capacity Is Already on the Books
text:
Caveats
Plan-enabled capacity is what the adopted plan makes room for, not a development forecast: it ignores ownership, market feasibility, and infrastructure timing. Densities use the midpoints of the Growth Policy’s designation ranges — the plan’s ceiling would roughly double the headline. Assessed values proxy price levels, not rents, so the NOAH flag marks relative affordability; the quarter-mile walkshed is straight-line, which slightly overstates walk access. The Sxwtpqyen master-plan area carries its own designation we conservatively treat as non-residential, so the true total is likely higher. See Methods & Sources.







Data sources.

City of Missoula taxlot layer (2024) with assessor, zoning, Growth Policy future land use, and constraint attributes (provided for this exercise)
Field map / data dictionary accompanying the taxlot layer
Mountain Line GTFS feed (stops and routes, July 2026)
American Community Survey 2019–2023 5-year estimates, Missoula city (tenure B25003, rent burden B25070)
Our Missoula 2035 Growth Policy designation density ranges, as applied in City annexation/rezoning staff reports; Our Missoula 2045 Land Use Plan housing targets

Analysis and figures: Kasey Zapatka, 2026. Full methodology: Methods & Sources. Code: github.com/kaseyzapatka/cascadia.

title: Interactive capacity map
text:
The value of this map is the overlay: turn on all three layers and you can see, block by block, where the capacity clusters sit in relation to public transportation — and which parcels drive each cluster.

Capacity clusters (green hexes) — areas holding significantly more plan-enabled capacity, counted with their neighbors, than a random arrangement would produce (Getis-Ord Gi*). The tiers are confidence levels, not capacity amounts: darker green means stronger evidence.
Opportunity parcels (blue) — the 3,419 vacant or economically underbuilt parcels where the Growth Policy already calls for more housing. Click any parcel for its current use, designation, acreage, and plan-enabled units.
Mountain Line bus routes (gray) — the transit network; 58% of all plan-enabled units sit within a quarter-mile walk of a stop.









Sources: City of Missoula taxlot layer (2024). Capacity is plan-implied (Growth Policy future land use), not a development forecast — see Methods & Sources.

title: Scaling to a Regional Housing Readiness Dashboard
text:
The primary data trap: schema fragmentation across jurisdictions. The pilot data already shows it — Zoning_Mstr mixes CITY -RM1-45 with COUNTY -Rural Residential, Small Agriculture-1: different naming schemes, different density logic, different vintages, in one field. Expanding to Missoula County and unincorporated Frenchtown, Lolo, and Bonner multiplies that: each jurisdiction’s zoning, future land use, and assessor attributes were built for different purposes, and unincorporated areas may have no adopted land-use plan at all. Naively stacking layers produces a dashboard that silently compares incomparable things — the most dangerous failure mode, because it looks finished.
The workflow to address it:

Canonical schema first. Define the region-wide analysis schema (the pilot’s derived fields: developable acres, plan-enabled capacity, opportunity class) before acquiring anything.
Per-jurisdiction crosswalks as data, not code. Each jurisdiction gets a version-controlled crosswalk table (source class → canonical class → assumed density, with a source citation per row). Crosswalks are reviewed with planning staff from each jurisdiction — the local-knowledge check no script can replace.
One automated pipeline. The pilot’s R pipeline generalizes: raw sources are never edited; every transformation is scripted; adding a jurisdiction means adding a config block and a crosswalk, not new code.
Validation gates between stages. Automated checks at each step — row counts reconcile, CRS uniform, geometries valid, no unmapped classes, capacity totals within plausibility bounds per jurisdiction — so errors surface at ingest, not at the client meeting.

Quality control before anything reaches the client:

Automated: the pipeline’s validation gates run on every rebuild; no hand-edited files anywhere in the chain.

Ground-truthing: for each jurisdiction, a random sample of ~25 parcels checked by hand against assessor records and aerial imagery.
Sensitivity disclosure: headline numbers published with their sensitivity to the key thresholds (density assumptions, softness cutoff), so no single assumption can quietly drive the story.
Sign-off checklist: sources cited, numbers reconciled to pipeline output, cartography standards met — before any deliverable ships.

Budgeted at blended rates:

Senior Associate — $150/hr × ~130 hours
Junior Associate — $95/hr × ~190 hours
GIS Intern — $55/hr × ~135 hours
≈455 staff hours ($45,000) plus $5,000 contingency (10%), sized to the real risk: other jurisdictions’ data
Invoicing tied to the milestone deliverable named in each task, not to hours

The budget’s shape reflects the risk: data normalization (Tasks 1–3, $25,000) is half the project, because the dashboard is only as credible as the crosswalks under it. The schedule’s critical path is jurisdiction response time — outside our control — so Task 1 secures data-sharing letters and a named contact per jurisdiction before analysis dates are promised. Scope boundary: the fixed fee covers the named jurisdictions and one dashboard revision cycle; additions are priced at the stated rates by change order. All required data is public and free (Montana State Library cadastral, city/county GIS, GTFS, ACS); commercial data, travel, and post-handoff hosting are excluded, with any records-request fees absorbed by contingency. The dashboard stays on an open stack — no per-seat licenses to inherit — and Task 6 ends with the client able to re-run the pipeline when next year’s assessor roll lands.
